text: Folly is foolishness, especially the expensive, well-meant kind — a course of action that sounds sensible and turns out to waste a great deal of money or effort. It is a heavier word than “mistake”, because it suggests the error was avoidable if anyone had thought it through. Calling free buses an economic folly is the headline’s way of saying the idea is popular, generous in spirit, and still a bad use of public money.

Immobility is the state of not being able to move. In writing about cities and jobs it usually means people who cannot get around easily — no car, no bus that goes where they need to be — and so cannot reach work, school or a doctor. The subtitle lists it beside climate change and inequality as one of the real problems free transport is meant to solve.

A leftie is an informal, slightly teasing British term for someone on the political left — a person who favours more government spending on public services, higher taxes on the rich, and stronger workers’ rights. It is the kind of shorthand a British magazine uses without meaning it as an insult. Here it labels New York’s mayor before the article has said a word about his policies.

A populist politician is one who builds support by presenting themselves as the voice of ordinary people against elites and experts. Populists exist on both the left and the right, and the label often carries a hint that the policies are chosen for how well they sell rather than how well they work. That hint is doing real work in this sentence: politicians, especially populist ones, love free buses because voters love free buses.

If something is all the rage, it is suddenly very fashionable and everyone is doing it. The phrase is old and usually carries a raised eyebrow, since fashions pass. Saying free public transport is all the rage sets up the sentence that follows: popular right now, and still terrible economics.

To proffer something is to hold it out and offer it, and in formal writing it almost always means offering an idea, an argument or a piece of evidence for other people to take or refuse. It carries a faint shrug that plain “offer” does not: what is proffered has been put on the table, not proved. That shrug matters here, because the three arguments supporters proffer are the three the rest of the article takes apart.

Investment here means spending money now on something that will keep paying off for years — new trains, extra track, more buses. Underinvestment is spending too little of it, so the system slowly decays and cannot grow. The argument being described is a chain: fares put people off, fewer passengers mean less money, less money means underinvestment, and underinvestment means a worse service.

Sparse means thinly spread out, with big gaps between the things you are counting — a sparse crowd, a sparse beard, sparse hair. A sparse bus network is one with few routes covering a lot of ground, so most journeys involve a long walk at one end. Paired with “low-frequency”, it describes the service nobody uses because it is barely there.

Ridership is the number of people riding a transport system, usually counted as trips over some period rather than individual passengers. It is the headline measure transport agencies live and die by, the way a website counts visitors. Almost every claim in this article is ultimately about whether making rides free moves ridership much, and the answer keeps coming back: barely.

A motorist is simply a person driving a car, and motoring is the activity of driving. The words are more common in British than American English, where you would more often just say drivers. Non-motorists, a few lines later, are the people without that option at all: the young, the elderly, the disabled, and anyone who cannot afford a car.

The social cost of an activity is its total cost to everybody, not just the bill paid by the person doing it. Driving to school costs you petrol and parking; it also costs everyone else a little more traffic, a little more noise, a little dirtier air, and a slightly higher chance of a crash. Economists add all of that up and call it the full social cost, and the complaint in this sentence is that drivers pay only their own share of it.

An externality is a cost or benefit that lands on somebody who was not part of the deal. The factory sells its goods and the neighbours breathe the smoke; a neighbour plants a tree and the whole street gets the shade. Because the person deciding never feels those spillovers, they do too much of the thing that harms others and too little of the thing that helps, which is exactly the argument being made here about congestion and pollution from driving.

The abbreviation ie is short for the Latin id est, meaning “that is” — it introduces a restatement of what you just said in plainer words. It is not the same as eg, which is short for exempli gratia, “for example”, and introduces one case out of many. Here ie is telling you what “physical activity” actually amounts to on a bus trip: walking, or sprinting for the stop.

Outside school reports, merit often means validity rather than praiseworthiness: to say an argument has merit is to say there is something genuinely right in it, whether or not you end up agreeing. Lawyers use the word this way constantly, as when a case is dismissed as being without merit. Granting that all three arguments have merit is how the article shows it is arguing fairly before it starts dismantling them.

Economic efficiency means getting the most total value out of the resources you have, with as little waste as possible. A bus running empty is inefficient in this sense: the fuel, the driver’s time and the vehicle are all being spent to move nobody. The efficiency argument for free fares is that the buses are running anyway, so filling the empty seats is pure gain.

A subsidy is money the government pays to keep the price of something below what it costs to provide. Nearly every bus and train system in the world is subsidised, so your fare covers only part of the ride and taxes cover the rest; a free system is simply one where the subsidy covers all of it. The article’s closing point is that the subsidy never disappears, it only moves from the passenger to the taxpayer.

In British English a scheme is just an official plan or programme, with none of the sneakiness the word carries in American English. The German scheme, the Estonian scheme and a pension scheme are all simply organised arrangements run by somebody. When a British writer wants the shady meaning, they normally say a scam or a plot.

At best means “taking the most favourable view possible”, and it almost always sets up a disappointment: at best marginal, at best a draw, at best a partial success. The phrase concedes the kindest reading and shows that even the kindest reading is not good enough. Its opposite, at worst, works the same way in the other direction.

Here marginal means so small it barely counts — an effect sitting out at the margin, the edge, rather than anywhere near the middle of things. Watch out for the other sense you will meet in economics class, where marginal means “of the next one”: the marginal cost is what one more bus ride costs to provide. Both come from the same image of the edge, but in this sentence the meaning is simply: the change in passenger numbers was tiny.

Evidence on the ground is evidence from real places where the thing has actually been tried, as opposed to predictions from a model or arguments from theory. The phrase comes from reporting and the military, where being on the ground means physically there rather than looking at a map. The whole article is a parade of on-the-ground evidence: Tallinn, Santiago, Germany, Luxembourg, Lens.

Price elasticity of demand measures how much the amount people buy responds when the price changes: percentage change in quantity divided by percentage change in price. Demand is elastic when a small price cut brings a big jump in sales, and inelastic when you can slash the price and sales hardly move. Public transport is famously inelastic, which is why Tallinn could drop the fare to zero and see trips rise only about 1% — most people are choosing on where the bus goes and how long they wait, not on the fare.

A referendum is a vote in which the public decides a single question directly, instead of electing representatives to decide it for them. Countries use them for constitutional changes and big one-off choices, and cities sometimes use them for things like transport funding. In Tallinn three-quarters of voters backed free public transport in a 2012 referendum, which is why the policy has such a solid mandate there.

Tallinn is the capital of Estonia, a small country on the Baltic Sea that was part of the Soviet Union until 1991 and is now known for how thoroughly it runs itself online. It made public transport free for registered residents in 2013, making it the largest city in Europe to do so. That makes it the longest-running natural experiment anyone can point to, which is why it opens the evidence section here.

In a randomised trial, researchers split people into groups by chance and give the treatment to only one group, so that any later difference between the groups is caused by the treatment rather than by who chose it. Medicine uses the design for drugs, and economists now use it for policies. Handing free two-week passes to a random set of Santiago commuters is exactly that: the people who did not get a pass show what the others would have done anyway.

Peak hours are the rush-hour windows when almost everyone travels at once; off-peak is all the rest of the day, when the same trains and buses run half empty. The distinction matters because a system has to be built for its peak, so off-peak passengers are nearly free to carry while peak passengers are the expensive ones. Santiago’s 23% jump appearing only off-peak is therefore a much weaker result than it first sounds.

This is a long-established academic journal for research on what governments tax, spend and regulate. Papers in it are peer-reviewed, meaning other economists have checked the methods before publication. Naming the journal is a way of telling you how much weight to put on the 35% finding that follows.

Capacity is how much a system could carry if it were full; spare capacity is the part of it currently going unused — the empty seats on a Sunday train. Filling spare capacity is cheap and genuinely useful, but it does not require anyone to build anything new. That is the article’s complaint about the German result: weekend trips to tourist towns used up slack that already existed rather than creating a case for more track.

As a noun, a pick-up is an increase or improvement — business picks up, the pace picks up, and the noun follows. It has nothing to do with collecting someone in a car or with a pick-up truck, which is the sense that usually comes to mind first. Here the initial pick-up in leisure trips is the early rise in people travelling for fun, which the phone-tracking data show faded quickly.

A working paper is research circulated before it has been through peer review, so other economists can read it and pick holes in it early. Findings in one are real work but provisional, and the numbers sometimes change before final publication. That status is worth remembering when you reach the Luxembourg figures, which the article immediately flags as carrying high uncertainty.

A stretched system is one already operating at or beyond its comfortable limit, with nothing held in reserve — the same image as a rubber band pulled taut. Nothing is physically being stretched; the word describes staff, trains and track all being used to the maximum. Add passengers to a stretched railway and you do not get a fuller railway, you get the 30% more delays reported here.

Two things go hand-in-hand when they have to happen together to work at all, like two people walking while holding hands. It is stronger than saying they often appear together: the phrase claims neither does its job alone. The argument here is that a fare cut only helps if extra services arrive alongside it.

A proponent of something is a person who argues for it publicly — the same role as an advocate or supporter, in slightly more formal dress. The opposite is an opponent, and the shared root in both words is the Latin for “to put or place”, so a proponent is the one putting the case forward. This paragraph is giving the free-fare side its reply before answering it.

Lens is a city in northern France, in a former coal-mining region, and its name is pronounced roughly like “lonss”, not like the glass in a camera. It is one of a number of French areas that have made local buses free. Ridership there jumped 40%, which the article credits to the extra services that came with the fare cut rather than to the fare cut alone.

Something patchy exists in patches — there in one spot and missing in the next, like patchy fog or patchy phone reception. Said of evidence or research, which is how you will most often meet the word in journalism, it means the studies do not line up: some find an effect, some find almost none, and some places were never studied. The verdict here is not that free transport fails to cut driving, but that the findings are too scattered to say confidently that it works.

Substitution is people swapping one thing for another when the deal changes — buying chicken when beef gets dear, or in this case leaving the car at home and catching the bus instead. It is the whole point of the climate argument for free fares, since the environmental gain comes only from journeys that move out of cars. Finding little substitution away from driving means the new passengers were mostly people who would have walked, cycled or stayed home.

To deter someone is to put them off doing something by making it look costly, difficult or risky — the same idea behind a deterrent, whether that is a lock, a fine or a nuclear arsenal. It works on the decision, not on the ability: a deterred driver still owns the car and could still drive. The question in this paragraph is whether a free bus is enough to put people off using it.

Luxembourg is a small, wealthy country wedged between Belgium, France and Germany, with fewer people than the city of Boston. In 2020 it became the first country in the world to make all public transport free nationwide. Being so small and so rich makes it an interesting test case and a difficult one, since almost nowhere else looks much like it.

A principality is a state ruled, at least in title, by a prince rather than a king or a president — Monaco, Liechtenstein and Andorra are the surviving European examples. Luxembourg is strictly a grand duchy, headed by a grand duke, but writers often reach for principality as a general word for one of Europe’s tiny monarchies. It is being used here simply to avoid saying Luxembourg twice in a row.

Nitrogen oxides are gases formed when fuel burns hot enough to make the nitrogen and oxygen already in the air combine, which happens inside every engine. They irritate the lungs, worsen asthma and help create the brown haze of city smog, and diesel vehicles produce a lot of them. They are a separate problem from carbon dioxide, which is why the Luxembourg study reports the two pollutants as two different numbers.

A tonne is a metric ton: 1,000 kilograms, or about 2,200 pounds, and slightly heavier than the American short ton of 2,000 pounds. Carbon dioxide is always counted this way, which can be hard to picture for a gas — burning a bit over 400 litres of petrol puts roughly one tonne of it into the air. Once emissions are weighed in tonnes, the cost of any climate policy can be written as a price per tonne and compared with any other.

In the European Union’s emissions-trading scheme, a power station, steel mill or airline must hand over one permit for every tonne of carbon dioxide it emits, and the total number of permits issued each year is capped and shrinks over time. Firms that can cut emissions cheaply do so and sell the permits they no longer need to firms that would find cutting expensive. Whatever a permit sells for, lately around 85 euros, is the going price of keeping one tonne out of the air — the number that makes the German ticket’s 6,140 euros per tonne look so bad.

Congestion pricing charges drivers for entering a busy area at a busy time, usually by camera and automatic billing, on the logic that a car in the centre at rush hour imposes delay on everyone else. London, Stockholm, Singapore and now New York all do it, and traffic drops noticeably wherever it is tried. It is the article’s preferred alternative because it puts the price on the thing you actually want less of, instead of subsidising a substitute and hoping people switch.

London’s ultra-low emissions zone, known as ULEZ, is an area where a vehicle dirtier than a set standard must pay a daily charge to drive at all. The aim is not to cut traffic in general but to push the oldest, most polluting engines off the road, and it now covers the whole city rather than the centre alone. The study quoted here credits it with cutting the share of London children with impaired lung function from 14% to 9%.

Impaired means damaged in function, working less well than it should — impaired hearing, impaired judgment, driving while impaired. It is weaker than “destroyed” and more clinical than “bad”, which is why doctors and lawyers reach for it. Impaired lung function in children means lungs that do not take in and move air as well as healthy lungs of the same age.

Low-earners and high-earners are simply people with small and large incomes from work, a neutral British way of saying it that avoids the loaded words poor and rich. The pairing sets up the fairness argument in this paragraph. A benefit that everyone receives, like a free bus, goes to high-earners too, which is why it can cost a great deal while helping the people who need it least as much as the people who need it most.

To accrue is to build up gradually over time, and the thing that accrues normally arrives in favour of somebody: interest accrues on a savings account, holiday days accrue as you work. It is a quiet, automatic sort of gaining, with nobody having to claim it. Saying the benefits also accrue to high-earners means the rich collect their share of the free rides without asking, simply by being eligible.

To cough up money is to hand it over reluctantly, usually because you have been asked one too many times. It is casual and faintly grudging, which is exactly the tone wanted here: a wealthy Londoner could easily cough up for a bus ride and simply is not asked to. The image is of something unwillingly brought out, the same way you might cough up a piece of food.

Loaded is slang for very rich, and it has nothing to do with carrying a load or loading a program. British and American English share this sense, and it is deliberately informal even in a serious magazine. A loaded City banker is the perfect example for the argument: the person least in need of a free ride is getting one anyway, at a cost to London of 220 pounds a year.

The City, capitalised, is the historic square mile at the centre of London where the banks and trading houses sit — Britain’s equivalent of saying Wall Street rather than naming a street. A City banker is therefore shorthand for someone with a well-paid finance job, in the way an American writer might say a hedge-fund guy. The capital letter is the whole difference between this and any banker in any city.

A boon is a benefit or a blessing, something that does you unexpected good. The word is old-fashioned enough that it now shows up mostly in journalism, usually in the pattern “a boon for” some group. It is set here against its opposite, a bane, to make one balanced point about public health.

A bane is the thing that ruins or spoils something, a lasting source of trouble rather than a passing annoyance. The word once meant an actual poison, which is why it still lands harder than “nuisance” and why the poisonous plant wolfsbane is named as it is; today you meet it mostly in the set phrase “the bane of someone’s life”. Free transport was a boon in Chile, where people walked more, and a bane in Estonia and Germany, where they walked and cycled less because they rode instead.

When one thing comes at the expense of another, the first gained only because the second lost — it is a trade, not a free gain. No money need change hands; the expense can be time, attention, health or, here, the walking and cycling people stopped doing once the bus was free. Watch for this phrase whenever a result sounds purely good, because it usually introduces the hidden cost.

To top something up is to add more to what is already there — a phone balance, a glass, a tank, or in this case a budget. It is standard British usage where Americans would say top off or refill. Germany charges 63 euros a month for the ticket and then tops the system up with about 3 billion euros a year of public money, which is the paragraph’s way of showing that no bus is ever really free.

Progressives are people on the political left who want significant social and economic reform, particularly in the direction of greater equality; in American politics the label marks the wing of the Democratic Party furthest from the centre. The word comes from the Progressive Era of the early 1900s, when reformers took on monopolies, corruption and child labour. The last line is aimed squarely at them: keep the ambition, drop the free fares, and buy faster buses instead.

Zohran Mamdani is the mayor of New York City, elected on a left-wing platform whose best-known promise was to make the city’s buses free to ride. The article opens and closes with him because he is the most prominent politician currently pushing the idea. Its closing observation is that he has already begun talking less about free buses and more about fast ones.

The Deutschlandticket is a single monthly pass that covers local and regional public transport anywhere in Germany. It began in 2022 as a 9-euro summer experiment aimed at easing energy costs, proved wildly popular, and became permanent at a higher price. Its cost has since climbed to 63 euros a month, and it still needs roughly 3 billion euros a year in public money on top.

A service described as thin is sparse and infrequent — barely any of it, spread over too much time or space. It is the same figurative thinness as a thin crowd or a thin schedule, nothing to do with width. Saying services are thin early in the morning and late at night explains why free fares help low-earners less than they look: the buses are free at hours when there are hardly any buses.
